title: Ohm's Law Explorer
objectives: Understand the relationship V = I × R
Measure voltage and current in a simple circuit
See how changing resistance affects current
description: Ohm's Law is one of the fundamental laws of electronics. It states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage and inversely proportional to the resistance.
steps: Place a 9V battery in the circuit
Connect a 1kΩ resistor
Add an ammeter in series to measure current
Add a voltmeter in parallel to measure voltage
Run the simulation and record V and I
Calculate R = V/I and verify it matches 1kΩ
Replace with 2kΩ resistor and repeat
questions: If voltage is 9V and resistance is 1000Ω, what is the current in mA?
How does current change when you double the resistance?
What happens to voltage if you increase current while resistance stays constant?

title: LED & Current-Limiting Resistor
objectives: Understand why LEDs need a current-limiting resistor
Calculate the correct resistor value for an LED
Observe what happens without a resistor
description: LEDs (Light Emitting Diodes) can be damaged by excess current. We use a resistor to limit the current to a safe level. The formula is R = (Vsupply - VLED) / ILED.
steps: Place a 5V battery
Connect an LED directly — observe it lights up very bright (dangerous!)
Add a 150Ω resistor in series with the LED
Run simulation and observe safe current (~20mA)
Try different resistor values and observe LED brightness
questions: Why does an LED without a resistor risk burning out?
If supply is 5V, LED forward voltage is 2V, and max current is 20mA, what resistor do you need?
What happens to brightness when you increase the resistance?

title: Series vs Parallel Circuits
objectives: Compare series and parallel circuit configurations
Calculate total resistance in each configuration
Observe how each bulb's brightness changes
description: In a series circuit, components are connected end-to-end and the same current flows through all. In a parallel circuit, each component has its own path and the same voltage appears across all.
steps: Build a series circuit with 3 LEDs
Measure total resistance and current
Observe LED brightness
Now build a parallel circuit with the same 3 LEDs
Compare measurements and brightness
Remove one LED from each circuit type — observe the difference
questions: Why do LEDs in parallel each glow brighter than in series?
What is the total resistance of three 100Ω resistors in series?
What happens in a series circuit when one component fails?
Why does a parallel circuit keep working when one branch fails?

title: Voltage Divider
objectives: Calculate output voltage using the divider formula
Build a potentiometer-based volume control analogy
Measure output voltage for different resistor ratios
description: A voltage divider uses two resistors to produce an output voltage that is a fraction of the input voltage. This is used everywhere in electronics — sensor interfaces, audio volume controls, reference voltages.
steps: Connect R1 and R2 in series from 10V to ground
Measure voltage across R2 (between the midpoint and ground)
Verify using formula: Vout = 10V × 7000/(3000+7000) = 7V
Change R2 to 3kΩ and predict new Vout before measuring
Try R1=R2=5kΩ — what is Vout?
questions: With Vin=10V, R1=4kΩ, R2=6kΩ, what is Vout?
How would you modify the circuit to get exactly 5V from a 10V supply?
How does a potentiometer act as a voltage divider?

title: RC Charging & Discharging
objectives: Understand capacitor charging and discharging behavior
Measure the time constant τ = RC
Plot the voltage vs time curve
description: When a capacitor charges through a resistor, the voltage rises exponentially. The time constant τ = R × C determines how fast this happens. At t = τ, the capacitor is 63.2% charged.
formula: Vc(t) = Vs × (1 - e^(-t/τ)), where τ = R × C
steps: Connect the R-C series circuit with the switch open
Close the switch to start charging
Observe voltage across capacitor rising
Calculate τ = RC = 10000 × 0.0001 = 1 second
Verify capacitor reaches ~3.16V (63.2% of 5V) at t=1s
Open switch to discharge through R — observe decay
questions: What is the time constant if R = 47kΩ and C = 220μF?
How long does it take for the capacitor to reach 99% of full charge (≈5τ)?
In which real-world devices do you use RC circuits?
